passage: Okay, Urmila, Sumit here, you asked how I got through the placement interview, so here's the strange part. I sat down, the panel started introducing themselves, and my heart was going like a drum. So I pressed all ten fingers flat on the table and spread them wide, like I was holding the wood down. It felt solid. My breathing slowed a little. One interviewer glanced at my hands and I thought, great, now they think I'm bored. But when they asked about my project I answered properly, and the interviewer nodded. Afterwards I told them I'd been steadying myself, and they laughed and said they'd assumed I was just being careful with the table.

qa.q: What did Sumit press flat on the table during the interview?
qa.a: Sumit pressed all ten fingers flat on the table and spread them wide.

qa.q: Why did Sumit spread and press the fingers on the table?
qa.a: Sumit was steadying nerves: the heart was going like a drum, and the breathing slowed once the fingers held the wood down. To an onlooker it could have looked like boredom, which Sumit briefly feared.

qa.q: What could an interviewer do if a candidate keeps pressing hands on the table?
qa.a: Judge by the answers rather than the hands, and perhaps offer a friendly opening question so the candidate can settle.

qa.q: How did the interviewer read the gesture in the end?
qa.a: The interviewer took it as carefulness with the table, not boredom, which shows one gesture can be read in more than one way.

grounding: A young adult presses spread fingers on a table to steady nerves and worries it looks like disinterest.

passage: Ritu here. Zubin sat at the end of our tutorial row on Thursday, and for the whole first ten minutes his hand was flat on the desk with the fingers stretched apart, pushing down. He didn't look at the board much. I figured he'd switched off, honestly, and I was a bit annoyed because he's usually the one asking questions. Then Professor Rao called on him and he answered perfectly, still pressing the desk with one hand. Later I noticed a small rubber ring in his other palm, which he turned round and round. I don't know what was going on for him. Maybe nerves about the test, maybe just how he listens. I've stopped assuming.

qa.q: What was Zubin's hand doing on the desk for the first ten minutes?
qa.a: Zubin's hand was flat on the desk with the fingers stretched apart, pushing down.

qa.q: What might Zubin have been feeling while pressing the desk?
qa.a: Most likely Zubin was nervous or restless, and the pressing and the small rubber ring helped him stay calm. Ritu admits it could also just be how Zubin listens, so the cue is not proof.

qa.q: What could Ritu do next time she wonders whether a classmate has switched off?
qa.a: Ritu could wait to see how the classmate takes part, or ask quietly after class, instead of deciding from the hand alone.

qa.q: How did Ritu's view of Zubin change after Professor Rao called on him?
qa.a: Ritu had been a bit annoyed, thinking Zubin had switched off, but after the perfect answer Ritu became unsure of the reason and stopped assuming.

grounding: An observer sees a classmate pressing spread fingers on a desk and using a fidget ring, and considers it may be regulation, not disinterest.

passage:
Dear Hansa,

You asked me last week why I was so upset after my internship chat, so here is the full story. I'd spent two evenings on the report. When I sent it, my supervisor replied with a single 👍 and nothing else. I stared at it for ages. Was that approval? Was it "fine, whatever"? My cousin says folded hands 🙏 would have felt warmer, but my friend Kabir says the thumb is just quick and friendly.

Today I finally asked her in person, and she laughed. She sends that thumb to everyone because she replies from her phone between meetings. So it was busy, not cold.

I still think I'll add a few words to my own replies. 🙂

Your friend,
Santosh

qa.q: How did Santosh's supervisor reply to the report?
qa.a: The supervisor replied with a single thumbs-up emoji and nothing else.

qa.q: Why did Santosh stare at the thumbs-up for so long?
qa.a: Santosh was unsure whether it meant approval or a curt 'fine, whatever', and had put two evenings into the report. The worry shows in the questions Santosh kept asking.

qa.q: What could Santosh do when a short emoji reply feels unclear?
qa.a: Ask the sender in person or in a friendly message what they meant, and add a few words to their own replies so others are not left guessing.

qa.q: Why did the supervisor send only a thumbs-up?
qa.a: The supervisor replies from a phone between meetings and sends that thumb to everyone, so it meant busy, not cold.

grounding: A young adult reads a thumbs-up emoji, finds it could seem curt, and learns the sender's habit differs.

passage: So, Tarun, it's Nilesh, you remember the group chat for our society event? I posted the poster draft and Meenakshi Ma'am, our faculty adviser, sent back a thumbs-up. That's all. Half the team said "yay, approved!" and the other half said it looked cold. I thought about it. My grandmother sends folded hands for everything, thanks, good morning, sorry about your cold, so to me that emoji is warm. The wave feels like "hello, I'm here". But the thumb? My friend Jai said in his office it means "seen, moving on", and in our class it means "great". Same little picture, different rooms. I ended up just asking Ma'am, and she said it meant she liked it.

qa.q: Who sent a thumbs-up to the poster draft?
qa.a: Meenakshi Ma'am, the faculty adviser, sent the thumbs-up.

qa.q: How did Nilesh feel about the thumbs-up?
qa.a: Nilesh felt unsure what it meant, since the team split between 'approved' and 'cold' and Jai's office reads it differently, so Nilesh weighed the readings and then asked.

qa.q: What would you advise a team that disagrees about what an emoji means?
qa.a: Ask the sender directly, in a friendly way, and agree on how the team will show approval in future.

qa.q: Why might Jai read the thumbs-up differently from Nilesh's class?
qa.a: In Jai's office the thumb means 'seen, moving on', while in the class it means 'great', so norms differ by workplace and group.

grounding: A young adult interprets thumbs-up, folded-hands and wave emoji and sees that the thumbs-up can seem curt in some settings.

passage: You want the travel story? Fine, Pooja, it's Irfan and here's the awkward one. First week in the hostel town, I got a nice fruit seller to laugh by making the OK sign with my hand, thumb and finger in a ring. Big grin, big thumbs-up, the whole thing. His face closed up. A woman next to him looked away. Later a local roommate told me that in some places that ring sign is rude, and the thumb can be too. Then in another city, a shopkeeper beckoned me with a curled finger and I thought, is this a hello or a telling-off? I had no idea. Now I just smile, say "namaste" with a small nod, and watch what people around me do.

qa.q: What sign did Irfan make to the fruit seller?
qa.a: Irfan made the OK sign, with thumb and finger in a ring, along with a big thumbs-up.

qa.q: What was Irfan feeling when the fruit seller's face closed up?
qa.a: Irfan was probably confused and embarrassed, since the friendly sign had clearly gone wrong. The face closing and the woman looking away suggest offence, though Irfan could not be sure at the time.

qa.q: What could a traveller do when unsure about a gesture?
qa.a: Smile, say a word or use a simple greeting like a small nod with folded hands, and watch what locals do before copying a sign.

qa.q: How might the fruit seller have seen Irfan's OK sign?
qa.a: The seller may have taken it as rude, even though Irfan meant it kindly, because the meaning of that ring differs from place to place.

grounding: A young adult travelling learns the OK-sign, thumbs-up and beckoning finger carry different meanings abroad and falls back on a smile and a neutral greeting.

passage: I'm Pooja, and Irfan and I were on the coach to the coast when he tried to thank the driver with a thumbs-up and the ring sign together. The driver stared, then said something short in his own language and turned back to the road. Irfan went quiet. I couldn't tell if the driver was offended or only tired, and I didn't want to guess out loud. At the next stop a woman from the tour told us that beckoning with one finger is treated as rude where she grew up. Irfan tapped his phone, looked up how people greet there, and after that he used a small smile and a nod. The driver nodded back at the end of the trip. Maybe that meant it was fine.

qa.q: Where were Irfan and Pooja travelling?
qa.a: They were on a coach to the coast.

qa.q: What might Irfan have been feeling when the driver turned back to the road?
qa.a: Irfan was probably embarrassed and unsure, which fits the sudden quiet. Pooja notes the driver might only have been tired, so the reaction is not proof of offence.

qa.q: What small step helped Irfan afterwards?
qa.a: Irfan looked up how people greet there and switched to a small smile and nod, a neutral gesture unlikely to offend.

qa.q: Why might the driver react differently from someone back home?
qa.a: In some countries the thumbs-up, ring sign or one-finger beckon can be rude, so the driver may have read them very differently from how Irfan meant them.

grounding: An observer watches a young traveller's gestures misfire across cultures and sees a smile and a nod work as a neutral greeting.

passage:
Dear Ujjwal,

You asked how the first month abroad is going, and I have a small funny story. In the lab corridor I wanted to call my lab partner over, so I did what we do at home: palm down, fingers scooping the air towards me. Nothing. He frowned, then came slowly with a puzzled look. Yesterday I saw a local student beckon someone with an upturned finger, and the person laughed and came straight over. Then in the canteen queue a staff member glanced at that same finger with a stiff face. So it isn't the same everywhere, even here.

I've decided to stop guessing. I use words now, "could you come?", and I watch what people do.

Miss you all. 🙂

Parveen

qa.q: What gesture did Parveen use to call the lab partner?
qa.a: Parveen used a palm-down scoop of the fingers towards the body.

qa.q: What was Parveen feeling about the beckoning puzzle?
qa.a: Parveen was amused but a little unsure, since the gesture got a frown from one person and a laugh from another. Deciding to use words and watch others suggests Parveen wants to avoid causing offence.

qa.q: What could a student new to a country do about unfamiliar gestures?
qa.a: Use plain words to call people, watch what locals do, and ask a friendly classmate what a gesture means.

qa.q: How might the lab partner have seen the palm-down scoop?
qa.a: The lab partner frowned and came slowly with a puzzled look, so the scoop may have seemed unclear or odd rather than friendly.

grounding: A student abroad finds beckoning gestures mean different things and chooses to watch locals and use words.

passage: Imran, it's Usha, remember when I told you about my first term in Norway? The funniest part was the beckoning. In my first week I called a course-mate over with the palm-down scoop we use back home, and she just laughed and said it looked like I was sweeping crumbs. Another time I crooked one finger upwards at a boy at the bus stop, thinking it was very casual, and he raised his eyebrows and stepped back. I felt my ears go hot. My housemate said in some places that finger is rude, or at least bossy. So I started asking, "Is it okay if I call you like this?", and I copied the way the locals waved. Guessing from home habits was the mistake.

qa.q: Where was Usha's first term?
qa.a: Usha's first term was in Norway.

qa.q: How did Usha feel when the boy raised his eyebrows and stepped back?
qa.a: Usha felt embarrassed, shown by the ears going hot, and realised the crooked finger had landed badly. The boy's reaction may also have been plain surprise, so it is a cue rather than proof.

qa.q: What would you advise Usha to do in a new country when calling someone?
qa.a: Ask politely, use a word or a wave that locals use, and avoid assuming home gestures will carry the same meaning.

qa.q: What was it like for the course-mate when Usha used the scoop?
qa.a: The course-mate found it funny, and said it looked like sweeping crumbs, so the meaning simply didn't carry over.

grounding: A student abroad learns that a beckon friendly in one place is rude or odd in another, and that asking and watching is wiser.

subtype: Signalling a turn in group discussion [Regulating]
passage: Seminar note, Thursday. Parul, a second-year student, sat at the far corner of the table during today's discussion on urban housing. When the argument turned to rent controls, Parul lifted one finger just off the table, leaned forward a little and caught my eye as chair. I nodded that I'd seen it and let the speaker finish. Two others talked over each other while Parul waited, hand still raised, jaw set. When the speaker paused I said, "Parul, go ahead." The point was clear and changed the direction of the talk. Afterwards Parul said the waiting was hard. I told Parul the signal was noticed and I'd keep a list of turns. I'll say that to the whole group next week.

qa.q: Which topic was the seminar discussing?
qa.a: The seminar was discussing urban housing, turning to rent controls.

qa.q: What was Parul feeling while waiting with a raised finger?
qa.a: Parul wanted to contribute and was likely tense or impatient, as the set jaw and the raised hand suggest. Another reading is that Parul was simply keen to make sure the point was not lost.

qa.q: What could the chair do to help quiet students claim a turn?
qa.a: Keep a visible list of turns and tell the whole group that raised fingers and leaning in are being noticed.

qa.q: How might the two who talked over each other see Parul's waiting?
qa.a: They may not have noticed the signal at all, or may have seen it and felt rushed, so a chair's clear turn order helps them too.

grounding: A young adult signals a turn by lifting a finger, leaning in and catching the chair's eye, and patient signalling gains influence.

subtype: Signalling a turn in group discussion [Regulating]
passage: Tuesday night, Naveen writing. Seminar today and I finally got a word in. I've been the person who blurts, so Suraj, the chair this week, had warned me last time. Today I tried something different. When Ananya started on the water policy paper, my hand went up a few inches, I leaned forward, and I tried to catch Suraj's eye. My heart was thumping and my foot kept jiggling because I wanted to jump in right then. I didn't. I counted two speakers. Then Suraj nodded at me and I said my bit, short. Priya said afterwards that it landed better than usual. I feel calmer than I expected, and a bit proud. 🙂

qa.q: Who was the chair this week?
qa.a: Suraj was the chair this week.

qa.q: What was Naveen feeling while waiting to speak?
qa.a: Naveen was eager and nervous, shown by the thumping heart and jiggling foot, and wanted to jump in at once. Holding back also shows Naveen cared about not interrupting again.

qa.q: What small step helped Naveen get a turn?
qa.a: Naveen raised a hand a few inches, leaned forward, caught the chair's eye and waited for two speakers before talking.

qa.q: How might Suraj have seen Naveen's behaviour this time compared with before?
qa.a: Suraj had warned Naveen about blurting, so waiting to be nodded at probably looked like better turn reading and more respect for others.

grounding: A young adult claims a turn with a lifted hand, a lean in and eye contact, and waits patiently instead of interrupting.

passage: Yosef's slides were ready, but his hands weren't. In the small seminar room in Haifa he stood beside the screen with a line graph of monthly rainfall and heard Noa in the second row whisper, "Slow down." He took a breath. When he reached the rise in spring, he drew his right hand upward in a smooth slant, then flattened it for the dry summer. It matched the picture. But when nervous, his left hand kept flicking a marker cap, and Noa saw two students watching that instead. After the talk she said, "The slope gesture was great. The flicking was distracting." He laughed and set the marker on the table. Next time he would record himself first.

qa.q: What did Yosef's graph show?
qa.a: The graph showed monthly rainfall.

qa.q: What was Yosef feeling as he presented, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Yosef was nervous, because his left hand kept flicking a marker cap. He was still able to use a clear slanting hand for the spring rise, which suggests he was also focused on explaining.

qa.q: What could Yosef do before the next talk?
qa.a: Record himself presenting on video, keep the gestures that match the graph and trim the marker flicking.

qa.q: How did Noa see the two kinds of hand movement?
qa.a: Noa found the slope gesture helpful and the flicking distracting, and noticed two students watching the flicking instead of the graph.

grounding: A young adult uses measured hand shapes to show a graph trend, while fidgety motions distract, and rehearsing on video helps.

passage: Dolma's turn in the lab meeting came after lunch. The supervisor, Dr. Mehta, had asked each student to explain their work in three minutes. She walked to the whiteboard and traced a rising curve with one finger, then made a small circle with both hands to show how the sample cycled through the machine. Anirban, sitting near the door, followed easily. Then her arms began to swing wide with every sentence, and he found himself watching the hands, not the diagram. Dr. Mehta wrote something down. After the meeting she showed Dolma a phone video from last week's practice. "See how the big swings start here?" Dolma winced, then grinned and said she'd keep the circle and cut the rest.

qa.q: How long did the supervisor give each student to explain their work?
qa.a: The supervisor gave each student three minutes.

qa.q: What did Dolma feel when she watched the practice video?
qa.a: Dolma winced first, probably embarrassed, then grinned, which suggests she took the feedback well and felt ready to change. The grin could also be relief at having a clear thing to fix.

qa.q: What went wrong in the second half of the talk, and what could fix it?
qa.a: The wide arm swings drew attention from the diagram; Dolma could keep the meaningful gestures and rehearse on video to trim the rest.

qa.q: What was it like for Anirban listening to the talk?
qa.a: Anirban followed the early gestures easily, but as the arms began to swing wide he found himself watching the hands instead of the diagram.

grounding: A young adult uses purposeful hand shapes in a presentation, over-large motions distract, and video rehearsal shows what to trim.

passage:
Monday. Yash met Aadhya at the campus cafe, where Aadhya's friend had introduced them. Aadhya is Deaf. Yash waved his arms and mimed drinking tea, thinking that would help, and Aadhya smiled politely but signed something quickly to the interpreter. Yash felt clumsy.

Thursday. Yash borrowed a book on Indian Sign Language, learned how to sign "hello" and "my name is", and read that the face, the space around the body and the movement all carry grammar. It is not mime. He realised his waving had been guesswork.

Next Monday. He signed "hello" and asked, using the interpreter, "Would you teach me some signs?" Aadhya's eyes lit up and both of them laughed.

qa.q: What book did Yash borrow?
qa.a: Yash borrowed a book on Indian Sign Language.

qa.q: What was Yash feeling on the first Monday, and what suggests it?
qa.a: Yash felt clumsy after his miming didn't connect, since Aadhya answered politely but turned to the interpreter. He may also have felt eager to be friendly, which is why he mimed in the first place.

qa.q: What could Yash do next to build the friendship?
qa.a: Keep learning basic signs, ask respectfully to be taught, and keep the interpreter's help until conversation grows.

qa.q: How might Aadhya have felt when Yash first mimed drinking tea?
qa.a: Aadhya probably felt polite but a little unseen, because signing is a full language and miming can seem like treating it as loose gestures.

grounding: A student learns that signed languages are complete languages using shape, movement, space and facial grammar, and respectful learning builds connection.

passage: I'm Nikita, and I'll tell you what I got wrong once, Tanuja, since you're starting at the college next month. When I was your age I shared a class with a Deaf girl called Rekha. I thought signing was just waving hands about, like charades. So I used big silly gestures at her, and I remember how patient her face was. Then her sister showed me a page on how sign language has its own grammar, faces and all, and I felt my cheeks burn. I asked Rekha to teach me a few signs, and she made me practise the alphabet till my fingers ached. We stayed friends for years. So don't guess. Ask kindly and learn the basics.

qa.q: What was the name of the Deaf girl in the elder's class?
qa.a: Her name was Rekha.

qa.q: What did Nikita feel when she saw the page about sign language?
qa.a: Nikita felt ashamed, shown by cheeks that burned, because Nikita had treated signing as charades. It could also have been a mix of shame and curiosity, since the next step was asking to learn.

qa.q: What would you advise Tanuja to do when meeting a Deaf classmate?
qa.a: Learn a few basic signs, ask kindly to be taught, and never treat signing as loose gestures or mime.

qa.q: How might Rekha have felt about the big silly gestures?
qa.a: Rekha's patient face suggests she put up with it politely, though she may have felt her language was not being taken seriously.

grounding: An elder recalls learning as a student that signed languages are full languages, and that asking respectfully builds connection.

passage: Note from Ms. Gurleen, peer-support tutor. During Tuesday's study group I sat behind the tables. Nilesh leaned back in his chair with arms folded, and for the first twenty minutes he said little while the others leaned in over the notes. A classmate whispered that he must be bored. I wasn't sure. Nilesh's face looked pale and he kept pressing a hand near his stomach. At the break I asked quietly, "How are you finding this?" He said he'd skipped breakfast and felt light-headed, but the topic interested him. We got him a snack and water, and he moved forward again afterwards. I'll remind the group that posture is a weak cue, and asking is better.

qa.q: Who did Gurleen sit behind during Tuesday's study group?
qa.a: Ms. Gurleen sat behind the tables while the group worked; Nilesh was one of the students there.

qa.q: What was Nilesh feeling while leaning back?
qa.a: Nilesh felt unwell and light-headed, but was still interested in the topic. The classmate read boredom, so the same posture had two possible meanings.

qa.q: What did Gurleen do that helped?
qa.a: Gurleen asked quietly, 'How are you finding this?', then helped get a snack and water instead of assuming disinterest.

qa.q: How might the classmate who whispered feel after learning the reason?
qa.a: The classmate might feel a bit sorry for guessing, and more careful about judging interest from posture in future.

grounding: A student's leaning back is read as disinterest but is actually feeling unwell, showing that posture is a weak cue and asking is wiser.

passage: Friday. Sudha was across from me in the canteen, leaning right back with her arms hanging loose, and I felt a small sinking. I'd been telling her about my project and I thought, she's bored. Earlier in the week she'd leaned in, chin on hand, so this felt like a change. I nearly stopped talking. Then I remembered what Mohit's brother says about posture being a weak cue, and I asked, "Am I rambling?" She laughed. "No, my back hurts from the long lecture, and I'm actually comfortable. Keep going." I was relieved, and I finished the story with her leaning back the whole time. Next time I'll ask sooner.

qa.q: Where was Sudha when she leaned back?
qa.a: Sudha was across the table from Mohit in the canteen.

qa.q: What did Mohit feel when Sudha leaned back?
qa.a: Mohit felt a small sinking and feared Sudha was bored, and even nearly stopped talking. The evidence is the sinking feeling and the comparison with Sudha leaning in earlier in the week.

qa.q: What small step helped Mohit find out what Sudha really felt?
qa.a: Mohit asked, 'Am I rambling?', a simple question that checked the guess instead of acting on it.

qa.q: What was Sudha's own reason for leaning back?
qa.a: Sudha's back hurt from the long lecture and she was comfortable, so the posture meant relaxed and not distant.

grounding: A student reads a friend's lean back as disinterest, then checks with a question and finds it was comfort.

passage:
Diary of Trisha. Exam day.

I sat down and the paper landed on my desk face down. Something in my body just stopped. My shoulders went up around my ears, my breath was stuck somewhere high in my chest, and my toes gripped my shoes. Deepika, next to me, must have noticed because she tapped her own shoulder twice and mouthed "drop them." I don't know how she knew. I let out one long slow breath, pushed my feet flat into the floor, and let my shoulders come down. My hand stopped shaking a bit. Then I turned the paper over and read question one. I still didn't know it, but I could think about it.

qa.q: What did Deepika do to help Trisha?
qa.a: Deepika tapped her own shoulder twice and mouthed 'drop them.'

qa.q: What was Trisha feeling when the paper landed on the desk?
qa.a: Trisha was anxious, shown by the raised shoulders, stuck breath and gripped toes. Trisha does not say it, but it could also be a rush of adrenaline before a big test.

qa.q: What steps helped Trisha settle enough to start?
qa.a: She breathed out slowly, pressed her feet flat into the floor and let the shoulders drop, which eased the shaking.

qa.q: How might Deepika have seen Trisha's stiffness?
qa.a: Deepika probably saw a friend frozen with worry and chose a quiet gesture, since speaking aloud in an exam would be risky.

grounding: A young adult stiffens and holds the breath in an exam, and slow exhaling, dropped shoulders and grounded feet ease it.

passage:
Rashmi: hey are you awake? 😰
Yash: yes why. viva at 9 right?
Rashmi: yes. I keep going stiff. Yesterday during the mock I stopped breathing mid sentence 😔

Yash: it helped me in my quiz. you don't have to be perfect, just steady
Rashmi: ok trying it now
Rashmi: ...honestly a bit better 🙂
Yash: good. tell me after

qa.a: Rashmi's viva is at 9.

qa.q: What was Rashmi feeling before the viva, and what shows it?
qa.a: Rashmi was anxious, shown by going stiff, stopping breathing mid sentence and having cold hands, and the worried emoji. Yash's reply suggests the stiffness is a stress reaction, though only Rashmi knows the full picture.

qa.q: What could Rashmi try before entering the room?
qa.a: Breathe out slowly, drop the shoulders and feel the feet on the floor, as Yash suggested.

qa.q: Why might Yash keep the advice so simple?
qa.a: Yash knows it helped in a quiz and wants Rashmi to feel steady rather than perfect, so a small easy step is more likely to be used.

grounding: A young adult stiffens and holds the breath under stress, and slow exhaling, dropped shoulders and grounded feet ease it.

subtype: Bowing, folding hands and formal movement [Mismatch]
passage: Note from Ms. Tanuja, exchange coordinator. During the welcome dinner for visiting students, I watched Zeenat greet the host family's grandmother. Zeenat put both palms together and dipped the head, a namaste, and the grandmother smiled and returned it. Then the host father, standing nearby, bowed slightly from the waist and held out a hand. Zeenat paused, looked at the others, and copied a small bow with a smile. Later Zeenat asked me quietly what the custom was for the elders. I explained that people here often stand when an elder enters. Zeenat stood up at once the next time. I'll add this to the orientation sheet as something to watch and ask about.

qa.q: How did Zeenat greet the host family's grandmother?
qa.a: Zeenat put both palms together and dipped the head in a namaste.

qa.q: What was Zeenat feeling when pausing between greetings?
qa.a: Zeenat was unsure which custom to follow and wanted to be respectful, which is why Zeenat looked at the others before bowing. The pause could also just be a moment of surprise.

qa.q: What could a visiting student do to avoid offending hosts?
qa.a: Watch how others greet, follow the local custom, and quietly ask a coordinator about the custom for elders.

qa.q: How might the host father have seen Zeenat's small bow?
qa.a: The host father would probably take it as polite effort, even if the depth was not exactly local, because it showed respect.

grounding: A young adult uses a namaste or bow according to custom, and learns to watch others and follow local custom to avoid offence.

subtype: Bowing, folding hands and formal movement [Mismatch]
passage: Diary. Rafiq here, late, sorry. Today at my cousin Vinita's engagement in Kyoto I got to see three greetings in ten minutes. Her fiance's grandmother bowed low, maybe thirty degrees, and I copied badly, too stiff. Vinita's aunt did a soft namaste, palms together, with a smile, and I did that easily. Then a young guy shook my hand and gave a short nod. I felt like a monkey trying to keep up, but nobody looked annoyed. Vinita told me later that the bow depends on who you are meeting, and that being sincere counts most. I'll still watch first and follow. Next time I'll bow a bit less rigid.

qa.q: Where did the engagement take place?
qa.a: The engagement took place in Kyoto.

qa.q: What was Rafiq feeling while trying to keep up with the greetings?
qa.a: Rafiq felt awkward and self-conscious, like 'a monkey trying to keep up', but also somewhat reassured since nobody looked annoyed. The relief is an inference, since Rafiq only says nobody seemed bothered.

qa.q: What small step helps Rafiq in the next such event?
qa.a: Rafiq can watch how others greet first, follow the local custom and keep a sincere manner.

qa.q: What did Vinita say about how the bow works?
qa.a: Vinita said the bow depends on who you are meeting, so the depth and manner vary, and sincerity counts most.

grounding: A young adult uses a bow, namaste or handshake according to custom and learns to watch others and follow local practice.
